summary: Defines how to carry NETCONF messages over SOAP, an XML messaging format common in web services, so existing web-service tools can manage devices. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4743 describes how to carry NETCONF device-management messages inside SOAP messages over HTTP or BEEP. The RFC is Historic and was updated by RFC 8996.

subtitle: The former NETCONF binding that carried management messages inside SOAP.

tldr.problem: NETCONF needed a mapping for environments that use SOAP web-service tools. SOAP provides a standard message envelope and can carry NETCONF XML messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4743 defines SOAP bindings over HTTP and BEEP. A NETCONF session follows the underlying connection, exchanges hello messages, and carries RPC messages in the SOAP body.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4743 is Historic and was updated by RFC 8996. Its transport mapping is not a current specification.

sections.title: Why Carry NETCONF over SOAP
sections.content:
NETCONF operations use XML and have remote-procedure-call characteristics, so the RFC maps NETCONF onto SOAP, an XML messaging protocol. SOAP has a standard envelope with a header and body; the binding places NETCONF messages in that envelope.

The RFC gives a practical reason for the mapping: SOAP over HTTP and its service-description tools were supported in many environments. It also notes that HTTP is client-driven, making server-initiated messages awkward, while BEEP supports exchanges initiated by either peer.
sections.plainLanguage: SOAP supplies a standard envelope for messages that already use XML. The binding lets existing web-service tools carry NETCONF requests and replies.

sections.title: NETCONF Sessions and Messages
sections.content:
A manager opens an HTTP or BEEP connection to a device agent and sends SOAP messages for a NETCONF session. With HTTP, the session starts when the first SOAP message is posted to the NETCONF application URI; with BEEP, it starts when the SOAP profile establishes a channel.

The peers exchange NETCONF <hello> messages to exchange capabilities and establish a session identifier. The HTTP client sends the first hello. NETCONF operations travel in the SOAP body, and closing the underlying connection or channel ends the session and releases its locks.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager opens a connection, and both sides exchange hello messages that describe their capabilities. The connection carries later requests and replies; closing it ends the NETCONF session.

sections.title: SOAP Faults and Service Description
sections.content:
When NETCONF returns an <rpc-error>, the binding wraps it in a SOAP Fault. The SOAP fault code is Receiver, its reason text comes from the NETCONF error-tag, and its detail contains the original RPC error.

The WSDL defines two operations, hello and rpc, using document-style literal message bodies. The SOAP header is not used to carry NETCONF metadata, allowing the NETCONF messages to remain similar across different transports.
sections.plainLanguage: A NETCONF error remains available inside a SOAP Fault, so SOAP software can pass it to the application. The WSDL describes the hello and RPC exchanges for software tools.

sections.title: Security, HTTP and Assigned Ports
sections.content:
NETCONF can read and change configuration, which may include sensitive information. The RFC says both client and server identities should be authenticated and the channel should provide strong encryption. Implementations must support TLS; the HTTP binding must support HTTPS, and the BEEP binding must support BEEP over TLS.

HTTP caches should not sit between managers and agents because session state is tied to the transport connection. The RFC specifies TCP port 832 for NETCONF over SOAP over HTTPS and port 833 for NETCONF over SOAP over BEEP.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuration messages can contain secrets, so the connection needs encryption and authentication. HTTP caches can break the session, and the RFC assigns separate TCP ports to the HTTPS and BEEP bindings.
